tools.title: Fighters vs. uniters and the big blue future
tools.summary_raw: The Democratic base is in a fighting mood. But Democrats now have a bigger tent to hold together.
tools.content_text: Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama at their Jan. 31, 2008 debate in Los Angeles. David McNew/Getty Images. As you may know, I’m fond of finding different ways to classify Democrats. Usually, this concerns the party’s voters, but in a New York Times story out this morning , I turned to their candidates. I have no problem with dividing the candidates into progressives and moderate “lanes,” particularly if one recognizes it as a spectrum rather than a strict boundary. But after spending a bunch of time last week binge-watching videos, debates, press appearances, and ads from 27 Democratic candidates — 13 leading 2028 contenders, plus 13 candidates who made major breakthroughs on Nov. 3 1 , plus Zohran Mamdani 2 — I don’t think that really captures the whole story. Instead, there’s another distinction that I call “fighter” vs. “uniter.” Graphic by the New York Times; ratings by Nate Silver. It really does help to watch the candidates in action to see this. Some classifications are obvious. Gavin Newsom’s whole thing is to fight back by any means necessary. When it came to leading Democratic efforts to fight Republican redistricting, I thought that was smart . I could do without his Trump-style tweeting, but I can understand why some voters like it. While “fighter” is correlated with “progressive,” the relationship is far from perfect. I consider Zohran to be a hybrid of “fighter” and “uniter,” but he’s closer to the latter end of the spectrum and often finds a way to signal that he wants to be a mayor for all New Yorkers, including through his consummately well-presented appearance. Conversely, I expected Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear to be fairly mild-mannered, and he often is, but look at him talking about JD Vance: There were a lot of cases like this. I classified only Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton as a pure uniter, a 7 on my 7-point scale. But you can watch someone like Mary Peltola get more and more worked up in her Oct. 15 debate against Dan Sullivan , for instance. In her opening statement, she described herself affably as a “lifelong Alaskan, a mother, a grandmother” — but by 10 minutes in, she’d gotten under his skin — and him under hers. “Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself for propagating these lies,” she said. Subscribe now I don’t want to preempt the NYT story too much, so go check it out . An undercurrent is simply how skilled some of the Class of 2026 are at communication. While James Talarico is perhaps the most obvious example of someone who can blend “fighter” and “uniter” styles, you’re seeing a lot of creative ways to bridge the gap, from Scott Colom’s use of humor to South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews playing the “I’m just a working mom and pediatrician” card in one commercial to some incredibly vicious attacks on the late Lindsey Graham (when he was originally her opponent) in another. tools.title: 9 Podcasts I’m Glad I Heard 🎧
tools.summary_raw: Memorable conversations about time, money, creativity, and connection, plus how I save the best moments
tools.content_text: Today I’m sharing nine of my favorite recent episodes. 🎧 First, my podcast toolkit I listen with the Snipd app , which lets me mark favorite moments. I triple-tap my AirPods or Sony XM6 headphones to highlight an excerpt. ( Why I use Snipd .) Snipd then emails me a summary of my highlights. Readwise hosts my collected podcast notes along with everything else I’ve highlighted while reading online or on my Kindle. Later, I query my clips with Claude or ChatGPT, using the Snipd and Readwise connectors, known as MCPs. (Here’s how that works .) This approach helps me find passages I liked and pull quotes like the ones below. Share Subscribe now 1. Time Sensitive Host: Spencer Bailey Standout episode: Oliver Burkeman on the Power of Embracing Imperfectionism I love this podcast’s focus on time. Bailey picks thoughtful guests and asks probing, surprising questions. His thorough research leads to questions other interviewers wouldn’t think to pose. is one of my favorite contemporary authors. I’ve adopted ideas from each of his books and I make a point of listening to his podcast interviews. So I appreciated that this conversation with Bailey felt different, like the two were venturing into new territory. In addition to covering Burkeman’s early career writing for The Guardian , they discussed why we shouldn’t obsess over others’ requests for our time and how to make peace with imperfection. Bailey is the founder of The Slowdown , a collective of writers, editors, photographers and others focused on quality over quantity. Another great episode: Maria Popova on the role of chance in shaping our lives . The intro to the podcast sums up why Popova ’s such a good guest: “The Bulgarian-born, Brooklyn-based … founder of the ‘free, ad-free, A.I.-free, fully human’ website and newsletter The Marginalian , braids together literature, science, philosophy, poetry, and art...” 2. How I Work Host: Dr. Amantha Imber Standout episode: Feel Stuck in Small Talk? Daniel Coyle Shares the Questions That Create Real Connection I discovered Daniel Coyle through this episode of ’s great podcast. He overflows with useful ideas. One of his books, The Talent Code , explores how top performers excel. In a video I like, he summarizes some of its most interesting takeaways. In his conversation with Imber, Coyle offers practical ways to move beyond small talk: ask better questions, try small community rituals, and notice what gives people energy. market.title: How reporters investigated pink slime news in small town Virginia

market.content_text: How reporters investigated pink slime news in small town Virginia By By Louis Hansen, The Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO | Published November 16, 2026 The Shenandoah Valley city of Winchester, Virginia, is like many small communities in America — it’s lost its journalists. In Virginia, 80 counties are now considered news deserts, with either one credible local news source or none. The local daily, The Winchester Star, recently cut staff, and the TV station has left town. Even the local university’s journalism program shut down. Enter the Winchester Gazette — and the town’s biggest mystery. The Gazette website launched in 2023 as a free alternative to the 130-year-old daily. The Gazette publishes daily stories about crime, government meetings and community events, some with the scent of AI text. It boasted of being the first website in the country to call the 2024 presidential election for Donald Trump. By one estimate, it had a monthly audience of about 11,000 visitors. Unlike traditional newsrooms, the Gazette’s stories carried no bylines. Its reporters, editors and owners remained obscured. Many community members had no idea about the who, what, when, where and why behind it. Our newsroom knew nothing about the Gazette. The Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO is a small nonprofit covering statewide stories for the public media station in Norfolk. One quarter of the newsroom is writing this narrative. We received an email tip about a possible story in Winchester, and I forwarded it to two trusted freelancers, Jaysun Silver and Laura Thompson. The email tip led nowhere, but days later it turned up almost verbatim in the Winchester Gazette. Silver and Thompson wanted to know more about a site that would publish a rumor, whose editorial policies were at odds with mainstream journalism. We saw more than a local story. The decline of local reporting, the ease of AI content creation, a community conditioned on free content and wanting local news – that’s fertile ground to plant an opaque, partisan news site. This could happen anywhere. We had long conversations with Jaysun and Laura. I gave them a template for a project proposal. What’s the story in one sentence? What’s the potential impact? Why does it matter to readers? We had a call every week. Those weekly talks kept everyone focused, allowed us to prune dead ends, connect with sources and push ahead as the reporting led us in new directions. Jaysun and Laura FOIA’d city emails for correspondence with the Gazette. They found more than a dozen stories on the Gazette website labeled “exclusive interviews.” They called the subjects. Several told VCIJ they had never spoken with the Gazette, yet were quoted extensively. They found a former Gazette reporter, who shared her contract with the news site. The agreement included a non-disclosure clause that called for up to a $100,000 penalty for revealing the operations of the Gazette. […]

market.title: Why The Times of India sees value in focusing on an ‘Adult Renaissance’
market.summary_raw: While news publishers mull over how to crack the Gen Z market, Mohit Jain, Chief Operating Officer of Bennett, Coleman & Co. Ltd., which publishes The Times of India, sounded a timely reminder not to ignore the Gen X audience.
market.content_text: By Joon-Nie Lau “Old has gold” Jain proclaimed before going on to elaborate on why an “Adult Renaissance” is taking place and why print is still alive in some parts of the world, particularly in India. Citing a World Economic Forum survey during question period following his keynote at WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit in Singapore in October, Jain said, “A Gen X spends about US$ 84,000 in the US and Gen Z spends half that,” emphasising the high disposable income that this demographic at the peak of their careers has. The AI of distribution For this media powerhouse that prints the world’s largest English language daily, The Times of India (TOI), and world’s second most widely read English business newspaper, The Economic Times, the acronym “AI” takes on a whole new meaning. “The most significant part is where are we selling,” said Jain, explaining TOI’s concept of the “AI” (Affluence and Influence) of Distribution that sells nearly three million print copies a day. “Let’s say Mumbai. While we may have an 81 percent market share of the brand audience, we have 90 percent market share in a city like Mumbai of the premium audience, like the people who are making a change in society—the top 1 or 2 percent of the whole demographic.” This approach is replicated across key cities like New Delhi, Bangalore and Chennai where TOI’s relative share in affluent areas ranges from 67 to 90 percent, even though its market share vis-à-vis competitors ranges from 51 to 81 percent. Bridging video, podcasts and print To attract younger readers and drive stickiness, there are 43 city editions of Times of India Metro Supplements (TIMS) such as the Delhi Times, Bombay Times and Hyderabad Times, packed with food, fashion, fitness, family, travel and Bollywood happenings. It’s a trendy metro lifestyle franchise that attracts over 2.6 million daily readers and 6 million followers on social media. Jain highlighted TIMS’ new multimedia extension launched last year – the popular Bombay Times Lounge celebrity video and podcast talk show which bridges the print coverage of the Bombay Times city supplement with digital and social storytelling for omnichannel distribution. For TIMS, this is a major revenue diversification initiative, allowing brand partners and sponsors to integrate into premium editorial entertainment content across print and digital platforms. On the digital front, TOI runs one of the world’s largest digital news platforms. Its own first-party Google Analytics clocks over 300 million monthly active users (MAU), about 25 percent of whom are international, with readers from the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom among its largest foreign audiences.
